summary:
Guernsey is a self-governing Crown Dependency with its own parliament, the States of Guernsey, and its own statute book. The United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and the single-sex services code issued under it in 2025 do not apply here automatically; United Kingdom measures reach Guernsey only by Order in Council.

Same-sex sexual activity is lawful for men and women. Criminalisation ended before 1983, when the age of consent was set at 21 in line with the United Kingdom; the male same-sex age of consent fell to 18 in 2000 and was equalised at 16 by legislation approved in 2011 that took effect on 5 November 2012. Guernsey nonetheless retains specific male homosexual offences in its criminal law, including a ban on homosexual sexual acts not conducted in private, which can expose men to prosecution for private-life conduct that is lawful elsewhere.

Transgender people have been able to legally change their gender since 2007, including obtaining a new birth certificate. Guernsey law only allows a new birth certificate to be issued and does not amend or remove records from existing birth certificates, so prior gender markers remain on the original record.

Guernsey is the only part of the British Isles never to have enacted civil partnership legislation, though United Kingdom civil partnerships were recognised for succession purposes from 2 April 2012. The States of Guernsey approved same-sex marriage on 10 December 2015 by a vote of 37 to 7, rejecting both a civil-partnership-only option and a single 'Union Civile' alternative; implementing legislation was to be separate and was not expected before 2017.

A 2004 law enabled the States of Guernsey to pass Ordinances banning discrimination, and the Sex Discrimination (Employment) (Guernsey) Ordinance, 2005 banned discrimination based on gender identity. As of 2020 no equivalent Ordinance had specifically outlawed discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation. Anti-discrimination protections covering sexual orientation and gender identity existed in child welfare proceedings in Guernsey and Alderney since 2008 and in Sark since 2016. In September 2022 the States of Guernsey passed a comprehensive anti-discrimination bill unanimously (33-0) explicitly including sexual orientation, rejecting all amendments proposing exemptions for small businesses of five employees or fewer and for religious affiliations; it takes effect from 1 October 2023.

Guernsey's only prison, Les Nicolles, opened in 1989 and holds male, female and vulnerable prisoners of juvenile and adult ages; it has 11 wings, capacity 139, is operated by the States of Guernsey, and held about 99 prisoners in November 2024. No rule on housing prisoners by birth sex versus gender identity, no separate unit for trans prisoners, and no solitary or segregation practice for them is recorded.

The States of Guernsey repealed the 50-year Adoption Law's ban on unmarried couples adopting on 24 June 2015, agreeing that same-sex couples may adopt, with civil partnerships recognised and equal parental responsibility for both partners; Jersey had approved the same change two days earlier. The Billet d'État of 24 June 2015 records the review of Adoption Law at p.1170, which led to adoption rights for same-sex couples.

Guernsey adopted the United Kingdom's relaxed blood-donor rules on 23 September 2011, making gay and bisexual men eligible after a 12-month deferral, targeted to around 7 November 2011 to match the United Kingdom change, ending the local 1980s HIV-era ban; other donation restrictions were unchanged.
tangentialFactors:
Guernsey's legal regime is distinct from the United Kingdom's: the States of Guernsey legislates directly, and United Kingdom equality legislation does not extend automatically. A trans visitor should not assume United Kingdom protections or the 2025 single-sex services code are in force locally.

The retention of specific male homosexual offences, including the ban on homosexual sexual acts not conducted in private, sits alongside an otherwise liberalised framework (equalised age of consent since 2012, same-sex marriage approved 2015, comprehensive anti-discrimination law from 1 October 2023). This combination means statutory text and lived practice may diverge.

Guernsey's approach to gender recognition, issuing a new birth certificate while leaving the original record intact, differs from jurisdictions that amend or seal prior records; visitors or residents relying on document consistency across borders should note that prior markers remain on the original record.

outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not document how Les Nicolles houses trans prisoners by birth sex versus gender identity, whether any separate provision exists, or what segregation or solitary practice applies; no rule, unit, or practice is recorded either way, which is an unresolved gap rather than a finding of safety or risk.

Whether Guernsey has a hate-crime statute covering gender identity or sexual orientation, and how the retained male homosexual offences are enforced in practice, are not sourced here.

Entry, visa, and border-screening treatment of trans travellers at Guernsey's ports of entry is not covered by this inventory.

The implementing legislation for same-sex marriage approved in December 2015 is referenced as separate and not expected before 2017, but the inventory does not confirm its final enactment date or current text.
